OFFICER TRAINING MEMO

You run the booth tonight.

Animals drive up to your checkpoint from the roads around the island. You talk to each driver, read their permit, and decide who gets in.

Step 1: Sort the clues. Every line of the conversation, and every thing you notice, is one of three kinds:

  • Quantitative observation: counted or measured. It has a number. "There are 3 animals in the car."
  • Qualitative observation: seen, heard, smelled, or read, with no number. "The car is red."
  • Inference: a conclusion built from observations plus what you already know. You did not see it directly. "The driver is probably in a hurry."

Step 2: Figure out where they came from, and where they are going. Drivers only tell you which road they used. Each sign on a vehicle fits more than one region, so no single clue is enough; two signs together point to exactly one. Use the road, the driving time, the signs, the cargo, and the Atlas tab (search it, or tap the Atlas button on any clue) to narrow it down. Only some regions are open each night.

Step 3: Approve or deny. Deny only when an observation or a solid inference breaks a rule on the permit or the border notice. A hunch is never enough.

Points: 1 per clue sorted right, 2 each for the right home region and destination, 3 for the right stamp, 2 for the right reason.

Add clues from the conversation or type in the search box; only regions matching every clue stay lit. Every region has things it is known for. Evidence on a vehicle tells you where it has been; cargo tells you where it is probably going.

END OF SHIFT REPORT

Shift complete

Remember: observations are what you counted (quantitative) or noticed (qualitative). Inferences are the story you build from them. A good inference, like figuring out a home region from a road and some mud, can be strong enough to act on. A hunch about a driver's mood is not.
